mathgap.title: Direct count assignment
mathgap.principle: When a statement explicitly gives a count for a person, set that person's current count to the given number, overriding any previous value. This assignment reflects the count at that point in the narrative.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement says "X has N items" (or similar phrasing).
mathgap.example: Adding the given count to the person's existing count instead of resetting it.

mathgap.title: Directionality of more/fewer
mathgap.principle: Interpret comparative statements correctly: "X has N more than Y" translates to X = Y + N, and "X has N fewer than Y" translates to X = Y - N. Preserve the order of the terms to keep the sign correct.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When encountering "has N more/fewer than" constructions.
mathgap.example: Swapping the terms and writing Y = X + N instead of X = Y + N.

mathgap.title: Split‑all handling
mathgap.principle: If a statement says that a person splits all of their items equally between two recipients, each recipient receives half of the original amount and the original person ends with zero. Apply the split using the current count at that point.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement mentions "splits all ... equally between" two people.
mathgap.example: Giving each recipient the full amount instead of half.

mathgap.title: Sequential transfer handling
mathgap.principle: Process each transfer in the order it appears: subtract the transferred amount from the giver's current count and add it to the receiver's count before moving on to the next statement.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement describes a transfer of items from one person to another.
mathgap.example: Applying all transfers using the initial counts and ignoring the order of statements.

mathgap.title: Signed difference substitution
mathgap.principle: When a signed difference (X − Y) appears in an equality and its numeric value is already known, replace it with that number to simplify the equation and solve for unknowns.
mathgap.when_to_apply: While solving signed‑difference equalities, after you have derived a concrete value for a difference.
mathgap.example: Leaving a known difference as a symbolic term instead of substituting its numeric value.

mathgap.title: Chronological evaluation
mathgap.principle: Read and apply statements exactly in the order they appear, because later statements refer to counts after earlier updates (transfers, assignments, etc.).
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains a mixture of assignments, transfers, and relational statements.
mathgap.example: Processing a later transfer before an earlier one, thereby using outdated counts.

mathgap.title: Conditional transfer handling
mathgap.principle: For a transfer that is conditional on a count, first evaluate the condition using the current count; only perform the transfer if the condition holds.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement includes a clause like "If X has more than N items, X will transfer ...".
mathgap.example: Executing a conditional transfer without checking whether the condition is true.

mathgap.title: Target variable dependency analysis
mathgap.principle: Identify which equations and variables directly or indirectly affect the queried person, and ignore all statements that cannot influence that variable, reducing the problem size.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains many statements, many of which are irrelevant to the final question.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire system of equations even though most variables never affect the target.

mathgap.title: Trivial signed difference detection
mathgap.principle: If a signed‑difference equality has identical expressions on both sides (e.g., (X‑Y) = (X‑Y)), recognize it as a tautology that provides no information and discard it.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When encountering a signed‑difference equality where both sides are syntactically the same.
mathgap.example: Treating a tautological equality as a constraint and trying to solve for variables.

mathgap.title: Signed difference equality parsing
mathgap.principle: Parse statements of the form "The number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of X that C and D have" as the signed equation (A − B) = (C − D), preserving the order and sign of each term.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a relational equality mentions "has more than" and "difference between" two other persons.
mathgap.example: Interpreting the equality as absolute differences or swapping the terms, losing the sign information.

mathgap.description: Treating signed difference statements as absolute differences or swapping term order
mathgap.why_it_happens: The phrasing can be misread, leading the model to drop the sign or reverse the operands, turning a signed equation into an unsigned one.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Parse the statement as (X − Y) = (A − B), keeping the order of terms and the sign of each difference.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model may treat all transfers as simultaneous, using the initial counts for each transfer instead of updating after each step.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Apply transfers one by one in the order they appear, updating the giver's and receiver's counts after each transfer.

mathgap.description: Assuming explicit counts are final after all transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: A direct count assignment is sometimes taken as the permanent total, overlooking later transfers that modify the count.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat a direct count as setting the current count at that point; later statements (including transfers) can change it.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The condition attached to a transfer is overlooked, causing the transfer to be applied unconditionally.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Evaluate the condition first; only perform the transfer if the condition holds true at that moment.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting multiplicative increase statements as additive
mathgap.why_it_happens: Phrases like "twice as many" are read as "N more than" and handled with addition instead of multiplication.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Recognize multiplicative relationships and translate them correctly (e.g., X = 2 × Y).
